title: Airport Pe ₹250 Ki Chai: Dukaan Wale Ko Kitna Bachta Hai?
description: Reasoning: 'why is X so expensive' is a universal, shareable curiosity. It follows the same structure as our mall-rent and railway-stall reels, with a 'who really gets the cut' reveal. Airport concession revenue-share figures are public via operator disclosures and tenders.
text:
HISAAB FACT SHEET: Airport retail and F&B economics in India (as of 16 Nov 2026)

HEADLINE FOR THE SCRIPTWRITER
- The data does not support a clean "owner is not the villain" twist. The landlord's cut is big and real. But India's biggest airport F&B operator also earns margins far above ordinary restaurant chains (see section 5).
- Safer framing: three players take a cut (govt, airport operator, outlet). The price is set by a captive audience plus a landlord who takes a % of every sale.
- I found no source for the cost of one cup of chai, and none for airport rent per sq ft. The sheet does not invent them.

1. THE PRICES (is ₹250 real?)
- Tea or coffee at airports is priced between ₹200 and ₹300. Basic thalis cost upwards of ₹500. [https://www.business-standard.com/industry/news/200-price-markup-at-airports-passengers-demand-affordable-options-survey-124121200896_1.html]
- One report puts a plain cappuccino at ₹250. [https://www.mypunepulse.com/chai-and-samosas-at-the-airport-can-be-quite-pricey-find-out-why/]
- Delhi Airport's own Dhaba page lists chaat items at ₹250–₹255. (Samosa Chat, Tamatar Chaat, etc.) [https://www.newdelhiairport.in/eat-and-dine/dhaba]
- A chai at exactly ₹250 is NOT verified. Use "tea/coffee ₹200–₹300" or "cappuccino ₹250".
- On the "3–5x" claim: one blog says airport tea costs 3-5 times the outside price. [https://successmarketingkota.com/blog/airport-food-court-packaging-requirements.html] The same page elsewhere says 2–4x, so it is a weak source.
- A better-sourced comparison is a LocalCircles survey. It found 60% of passengers were charged 100–200% more than at railway stations. [https://www.localcircles.com/a/press/page/airport-food-prices]
- Safer on-screen wording: "2–4x" or "double to triple".

2. HOW OUTLETS WIN SPACE (tender and rent model)
- Concession agreements require the operator to pay a % of revenue or a minimum guaranteed amount, whichever is higher. [https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/ADV_INE103V01028_11JUL2025.pdf]
- Meaning: if sales are poor, the outlet still pays the minimum. If sales are great, the airport takes a % of the upside.
